title: 'Dai Dai' Dominates: Shakira & Burna Boy's World Cup Anthem Holds #1, Ariana Grande Rebounds on Global Charts
summary: The World Cup isn't just dominating soccer fields — it's taking over global music charts. Shakira and Burna Boy's 'Dai Dai (FIFA World Cup Official Song 2026)' has secured a second consecutive week at No. 1 on the Billboard Global Excl. U.S. chart, which ranks songs based on streaming and sales from over 200 territories outside the United States. A week earlier, it became the first official World Cup anthem to ever top the ranking since it launched in 2020. The song's momentum was fueled by a live performance at the FIFA World Cup 2026 opening ceremony on June 11 at Mexico City's Estadio Azteca, where a reported 80,000-plus fans witnessed the spectacle. As the tournament barrels toward its July 19 finale, anticipation is building for the first-ever World Cup final halftime show at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where Shakira will be joined by BTS and Madonna. On the Billboard Global 200 — which includes worldwide data, including the U.S. — Ariana Grande's 'Hate That I Made You Love Me' rebounded to No. 1 for a second non-consecutive week. This ties her longest reign among her four chart-toppers, matching 'Yes, And?' in 2024 and 'Positions' in 2020. The track had previously spent its first two weeks at No. 1 in June before dipping, but now it's back on top. Meanwhile, 'Dai Dai' surged 9-3 on the Global 200, showing its cross-border appeal. BTS' 'Swim' holds at No. 2 on Global Excl. U.S. after an eight-week run at the summit since April, while Michael Jackson's 'Billie Jean' and Justin Bieber's 'Beauty and a Beat' remain in the top five. A notable milestone: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' finally cracked the top five on the Global 200 after 36 weeks — the longest climb to the region for a song by a female artist with no other billed acts. The charts, dated July 11, 2026, are compiled by Luminate using a weighted formula that includes official streams and download sales, with direct-to-consumer purchases excluded. The full 200-title rankings are available on Billboard Pro, while the top 100 are free to all readers. With the World Cup still in full swing, 'Dai Dai' might just have the legs to keep its crown — and the closing ceremony could give it another boost. For now, it's clear that the intersection of sports and music has never been louder.
why_it_matters: For a generation that streams music globally, this story shows how mega-events like the World Cup can reshape listening habits overnight and turn a song into a worldwide phenomenon—demonstrating the economic and cultural power of live sports as marketing platforms.

keywords.explanation: In this context, 'territories' means countries or regions that are treated as separate markets for tracking music streams and sales.
Non-consecutive means something did not happen in back-to-back weeks; here it means the song was No. 1, dropped down, and then returned to No. 1.
Momentum is the energy or force that helps something continue moving forward once it has started.
Cross-border appeal means a song is popular across many different countries, not just in one place.
Chart-toppers are songs that reach the number one position on a music ranking list.
A weighted formula is a calculation that gives different levels of importance to different numbers, like counting streams more than downloads.

background_read: FIFA (the Fédération Internationale de Football Association, founded in 1904) has used official World Cup songs since 1962 to promote the tournament; past anthems like Shakira's 'Waka Waka' (2010) became global hits.

The Billboard charts have been the music industry's standard ranking system since 1940. In 2020, they launched the Global 200 and Global Excl. U.S. charts to reflect worldwide streaming and sales data, tracking songs from over 200 territories.

Estadio Azteca, where the opening ceremony was held, is a historic 87,000-seat stadium in Mexico City that previously hosted the World Cup finals in 1970 and 1986, making it the first venue to host three World Cup openers.

MetLife Stadium, the site of the 2026 final, is an 82,500-capacity venue in New Jersey that is home to two NFL teams and has been chosen to add a Super Bowl–style halftime show to the World Cup for the first time.

Luminate, formerly known as Nielsen SoundScan, is the data company that tracks music consumption for Billboard; its formulas give different weights to paid streams, ad-supported streams, and digital downloads.
Article_Structure: LEAD: The World Cup is dominating not just sports but global music charts, signaling a powerful crossover moment.
KEY STORY: 'Dai Dai' by Shakira and Burna Boy secures a second week at No. 1 on the Billboard Global Excl. U.S. chart.
├─ HISTORIC FEAT: It's the first official World Cup anthem to top this ranking since its 2020 launch.
└─ CATALYST: A live performance at the opening ceremony in front of 80,000+ fans in Mexico City.
FUTURE EVENT: Anticipation builds for the first-ever World Cup final halftime show at MetLife Stadium in July.
└─ LINEUP: Shakira joined by BTS and Madonna, promising another chart boost.
BROADER CONTEXT: The Billboard Global 200 includes U.S. data and shows Ariana Grande's 'Hate That I Made You Love Me' rebounding to No. 1.
├─ DETAIL: It ties her longest reign among her four chart-toppers.
└─ CROSSOVER: 'Dai Dai' surges 9-3 on this global chart, proving broad appeal.
OTHER PLAYERS: BTS' 'Swim' holds at No. 2 on Global Excl. U.S.; legacy hits by Michael Jackson and Justin Bieber remain in the top five.
MILESTONE: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' cracks top five after 36 weeks, a record slow climb for a solo female artist.
BEHIND THE NUMBERS: Charts compiled by Luminate using a weighted formula of streams and downloads, excluding direct-to-consumer sales.
OUTLOOK: With the tournament ongoing and a closing ceremony ahead, 'Dai Dai' may keep its crown.

perspectives.description: Shakira and Burna Boy gain unprecedented global exposure tied to the world's biggest sporting event, while FIFA's halftime show idea modernizes the tournament and creates new revenue and fan engagement streams.

Critics argue that manufactured event songs often lack artistic merit and quickly fade; the heavy commercialization of sports events may also oversaturate audiences and dilute genuine cultural moments.

Chart dynamics reveal the fragmented nature of global music consumption—a song can dominate outside the U.S. while a different track leads globally, showing how streaming data now paints a multi-polar entertainment landscape rather than one American-centered hit machine.

If the halftime show becomes a permanent fixture, future World Cups may increasingly blend sports and entertainment, potentially altering both industries. This could open doors for more global artists but also raise questions about authenticity when sport becomes a stage for profit.
